Micro-aeration enhances lactic acid production in food waste fermentation
Luxin Yang , Chuyun Zhao , Caiping Sun , Huan Li *
Tsinghua Shenzhen International Graduate School, Tsinghua University, Shenzhen 518055, China
H I G H L I G H T S
G R A P H I C A L  A B S T R A C T
• Low-to-moderate micro-aeration signif­
icantly enhances lactic acid fermenta­
tion of food waste.
• An aeration rate of 327  mL air/(gVS⋅L) 
achieved the highest steady-state lactic 
acid concentration.
• Micro-aeration promoted the activity 
of 
homofermentative 
Lactobacillus 
amylolyticus.
• Fungal oxidative phosphorylation and 
TCA cycle activity were stimulated 
under micro-aeration.
• Heterofermentative 
LAB 
lost 
their 
competitive advantage under micro- 
aerobic conditions.
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Organic waste
Organic acid
Oxygen response
Biological treatment
Microbial metabolism
Metatranscriptomics
A B S T R A C T
Micro-aeration is a promising strategy to enhance hydrolysis and acidogenesis in anaerobic fermentation sys­
tems, but its role in lactic acid (LA) fermentation of food waste (FW) remains unclear. Here, four 1.5-L semi- 
continuous reactors (35 ◦C, HRT = 3 d) were run at dissolved oxygen < 0.5 mg/L with aeration loads of 0, 
109, 327 and 872 mL air/(gVS⋅L). Moderate aeration (327 mL air/(gVS⋅L)) increased steady-state LA to 17.68 ±
1.14 g/L (0.40 g/gVS), 35.5 % higher than strict anaerobiosis, with LA contributing > 85 % of product COD and 
maximum hydrolysis and acidification efficiencies. In contrast, excessive aeration (872 mL air/(gVS⋅L)) 
decreased LA yield. Amplicon and metatranscriptomic analyses showed that micro-aeration enriched homo­
fermentative Lactobacillus amylolyticus and activated pyruvate oxidase–acetyl phosphate–acetate and NADH 
peroxidase pathways, enhancing redox balancing and starch hydrolysis. Overall, controlled micro-aeration 
steered metabolism toward energy-efficient homofermentative LAB, improving LA yield and process stability.
1. Introduction
Anaerobic biological treatment is a widely adopted strategy for 
managing organic solid waste. In the absence of oxygen, anaerobic mi­
croorganisms degrade organic matter into low-molecular-weight prod­
ucts to obtain energy for their metabolism and growth (Zhang et al., 
2014; Zhou et al., 2018). These biochemical processes allow for the 
valorization of organic waste into a range of high-value products, such 
as methane (CH4), hydrogen (H2), organic acids, etc., making this 
approach particularly attractive for resource recovery from a wide range 
of substrates, including agricultural residues, food waste (FW), and 
herbal-medicine by-products. (Prasanna Kumar et al., 2024; Wang et al.,

Among various anaerobic treatment technologies, anaerobic diges­
tion (AD) is the most widely implemented due to its high conversion 
efficiency and energy recovery potential. It is governed by four succes­
sive and tightly interlinked microbial steps: hydrolysis, acidogenesis, 
acetogenesis, and methanogenesis (Ren et al., 2018). Traditionally, AD 
is regarded as requiring strict anaerobic operating conditions, mainly 
owing to the high oxygen sensitivity of methanogens. Specifically, the 
key metabolic enzymes of these organisms, such as methyl-coenzyme M 
reductase, harbor low-redox-potential metal cofactors (e.g., Ni and Fe) 
that are highly susceptible to oxidative inactivation (Thauer, 2019). 
Moreover, intracellular oxygen can generate reactive oxygen species 
(ROS), such as superoxide (O2
–) and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), leading 
to secondary oxidative damage (Lu and Imlay, 2021). Beyond metha­
nogens, syntrophic bacteria responsible for converting longer-chain 
volatile fatty acids into acetic acid, H2, and CO2 have also been re­
ported to be highly sensitive to oxygen (Magalh˜aes et al., 2025). Theo­
retically, even trace amounts of O2 can disrupt the low hydrogen partial 
pressures essential for syntrophic metabolism and inhibit the activity of 
key hydrogenases (Sieber et al., 2012). Collectively, based on traditional 
theories, the presence of oxygen in AD systems can significantly reduce 
microbial activity, impair the acetogenic and methanogenic functions of 
the microbial community, and ultimately lead to decreased methane 
yields.
However, in recent years, a growing body of research has demon­
strated that micro-aeration can enhance the performance of AD. Among 
the four stages of AD, micro-aeration can stimulate hydrolysis and 
acidogenesis. Specifically, it can activate hydrolytic bacterial commu­
nities to produce higher levels of extracellular enzymes such as amy­
lases, proteases, and cellulases, thereby accelerating the breakdown of 
macromolecular substrates (Johansen and Bakke, 2006; Sawatdeenar­
unat et al., 2017). This enzymatic enhancement increases the avail­
ability of monomers for fermentative bacteria, facilitating the 
production of volatile fatty acids (VFAs) and other fermentation prod­
ucts (Yin et al., 2016). Acetogenesis is thermodynamically unfavorable. 
If its progress is slowed or inhibited, intermediate short-chain fatty acids 
(SCFAs), particularly propionic acid and butyric acid, may accumulate 
(Han et al., 2020). Trace amounts of oxygen (O2) have been shown to 
stimulate the conversion of SCFAs into acetic acid, thereby increasing 
the availability of substrates for methanogens (Lim and Wang, 2013). 
Furthermore, under controlled aeration rates, facultative bacteria can 
directly utilize O2 to oxidize VFAs into CO2, thereby mitigating VFA 
accumulation and alleviating pH-induced inhibition of methanogenic 
archaea (Nguyen et al., 2019). Importantly, oxygen introduced through 
micro-aeration is rapidly consumed by facultative microorganisms, 
thereby maintaining an anaerobic environment suitable for methano­
genesis (Nguyen and Khanal, 2018). As a result, micro-aeration does not 
inhibit the AD process; on the contrary, it can promote methanogenic 
activity, improve system stability, and enhance methane yields (Jenicek 
et al., 2014; Li et al., 2024). Given its ability to stimulate hydrolysis and 
acidogenesis, micro-aeration holds potential not only for enhancing 
biogas production but also for application in anaerobic fermentation 
systems where high-value organic acids are the desired end products.
In recent years, this concept has been extended from biogas-oriented 
AD to acidogenic fermentation processes aimed at producing organic 
acids. Although the body of work remains relatively limited, several 
studies have reported that micro-aeration can enhance organic acid 
production. Wen et al. (2022) reported that micro-aeration increased the 
yield of VFAs from activated sludge fermentation by more than twofold 
and significantly elevated the proportion of acetic acid. Cao et al. 
(2022b) conducted acidogenic fermentation using agricultural waste as 
the substrate and found that micro-aeration inhibited the conversion of 
lactic acid (LA) into VFAs, thereby improving LA accumulation. Simi­
larly, Liao et al. (2025) also confirmed that micro-aeration strategies can 
promote LA production during the fermentation of herbal waste. These 
studies indicate that low-level oxygen inputs can be harnessed to steer 
carbon flux toward specific acidogenic products, including LA.
FW constitutes a major fraction of municipal solid waste and con­
tinues to increase globally, posing substantial challenges for urban waste 
management. AD is widely used for FW treatment due to its operational 
reliability and energy-recovery capability (Yang et al., 2023); however, 
it requires long hydraulic retention times (HRTs) and is highly sensitive 
to environmental disturbances such as the accumulation of free 
ammonia and VFAs (Prasanna Kumar et al., 2024). In contrast, anaer­
obic fermentation for LA has recently emerged as a promising strategy to 
enhance the resource recovery value of FW (Wang et al., 2020). LA has 
broad applications in the chemical and feed industries and serves as a 
key monomer for polylactic acid (PLA), a widely used biodegradable 
polymer (L´opez-G´omez et al., 2019). To date, various strat­
egies—including temperature optimization (Tang et al., 2016), pH 
control (Hussain et al., 2017), specialized inocula (Arras et al., 2019), 
and regulation of the organic loading rate (OLR) (Jiang et al., 2013)— 
have been investigated to improve FW-to-LA conversion. However, 
existing micro-aeration studies on LA production have focused on 
agricultural residues or herbal waste, and micro-aerated LA fermenta­
tion from FW has not yet been explored. Moreover, the mechanistic basis 
of micro-aeration in AF systems remains poorly understood, and gene- 
expression-level insights into community metabolism and functional 
dynamics are critically needed.
In this study, we investigated the effects of different aeration rates on 
LA production from FW fermentation, with the aim of determining 
optimal aeration parameters. Meanwhile, 16S rRNA gene and Internal 
Transcribed Spacer (ITS) amplicon sequencing were conducted to 
examine bacterial and fungal community structures under varying 
aeration conditions. In addition, metatranscriptomic analysis was 
employed to assess the impact of aeration on microbial gene expression, 
thereby providing deeper insights into the mechanisms by which micro- 
aeration enhances LA fermentation. This study not only advances our 
understanding of micro-aeration as a fermentation strategy but also 
contributes to the mechanistic foundation and practical optimization of 
micro-aeration for broader applications in anaerobic bioprocess 
engineering.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Substrate and inoculum
To keep the feedstock identical across the whole experimental 
period, simulated FW was used in the experiment. The full-price com­
mercial dog food (Sam’s Club, USA) and polished white rice were mixed 
at a mass ratio of 1:1, followed by the addition of water for cooking. 
Subsequently, the mixture was crushed using a wall-breaking machine 
into a pulp with an average particle size of less than 0.5 mm. The pulp, 
after homogenization, was stored in a refrigerator at –20◦C. Before use, 
it was thawed, and its total solid content was adjusted to approximately 
5.0 ± 0.2 % using tap water as feedstock. The characteristics of the 
feedstock are shown in Table 1. Biogas slurry used for inoculation was 
obtained from a FW treatment plant employing mesophilic anaerobic

2.2. Reactor set-up and operation
Fermentation experiments were conducted in four glass reactors, 
each with a working volume of 1,500 mL. Each glass reactor was fitted 
with two 3 mm-diameter ports at the top, functioning as the air inlet and 
outlet, respectively. The outer side of the air inlet port was connected to 
a peristaltic pump (LongerPump BT100-3 J, Longer Pump Co., Ltd., 
China) to supply air into the reactor, while the inner side was connected 
to a circular high-pressure microporous ceramic diffuser (QL113-0, 130 
× 130 mm; Qili Environmental Protection, China). It dispersed the 
incoming air into fine bubbles with an average diameter of less than 0.5 
mm, as specified by the manufacturer. Four aeration rates (the volu­
metric airflow supplied per unit time) were applied: 0, 5.0, 15.0, and 
40.0 mL/min, corresponding to reactors A0, A5, A15, and A40, 
respectively. A magnetic stir bar was placed in each reactor, and all 
reactors were immersed in a thermostatic water bath equipped with 
magnetic stirring. The stirring speed was maintained at 60 rpm, and the 
temperature was controlled at 35.0 ± 1.0◦C. At the start of the experi­
ment, each reactor was loaded with 1,400  mL of substrate and 100  mL 
of inoculum, resulting in an effective working volume of 1,500  mL. To 
investigate the effect of aeration on rapid LA fermentation with a high 
dilution rate, the reactors were operated in a semi-continuous mode 
with a HRT of 3 days. Each day, 500  mL of fermentation broth was 
withdrawn and replaced with fresh feedstock, corresponding to an OLR 
of 14.7 g VS/(L⋅d). The fermentation experiment lasted for a total of 22 
days. Effluent samples were collected every two days for subsequent 
analysis.
2.3. Fermentation degree
Fermentation degrees can be expressed using hydrolysis rate (HR) 
and acidogenic rate (AR). These parameters reflect the extent to which 
solid substrates are solubilized and further converted into fermentation 
products. They were calculated as follows: 
HR = (SCOD/TCOD) × 100%
(1) 
AR = (CODp/TCOD) × 100%
(2) 
where SCOD is the soluble chemical oxygen demand of fermentation 
effluent, TCOD is the total chemical oxygen demand of feedstock, and 
CODp is the sum of COD for the fermentation products.
2.4. Microbial analysis
On the final day of the experiment (steady-state), fermentation broth 
samples were collected, immediately frozen in liquid nitrogen, and 
stored in a liquid nitrogen tank to preserve sample integrity. The frozen 
samples were then shipped to Majorbio Inc. (Shanghai, China) for DNA/ 
RNA extraction and sequencing.
To analyze microbial diversity, total DNA was extracted using the 
PowerSoil® DNA Isolation Kit (Mo Bio Laboratories Inc., Carlsbad, USA) 
and amplified with a PCR thermocycler (GeneAmp® 9700, ABI, USA). 
For bacteria, the primer pair 338F (5′-ACTCCTACGGGAGGCAGCAG-3′) 
and 806R (5′-GGACTACHVGGGTWTCTAAT-3′) was used, while for eu­
karyotes such as fungi, ITS1F (5′-CTTGGTCATTTAGAGGAAGTAA-3′) 
and ITS2R (5′-GCTGCGTTCTTCATCGATGC-3′) were used. PCR products 
were purified and sequenced on an Illumina MiSeq platform (Illumina, 
USA). Sequence data were processed and analyzed using the QIIME 2 
software package.
For metatranscriptomic analysis, total RNA was extracted and puri­
fied using the Soil RNA Extraction Kit (Majorbio, Shanghai, China) 
following the manufacturer’s instructions. RNA concentration and 
integrity were assessed using a NanoDrop 2000 spectrophotometer 
(Thermo Scientific, MA, USA) and an Agilent 5300 Bioanalyzer (Agilent 
Technologies, Palo Alto, CA, USA). RNA libraries were prepared using 
the Illumina® Stranded mRNA Prep Ligation Kit (Illumina, San Diego, 
CA, USA), and ribosomal RNA was removed using the RiboCop rRNA 
Depletion Kit for Mixed Bacterial Samples (Lexogen, USA). Paired-end 
(150 bp) sequencing was performed on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 
platform at Majorbio Bio-Pharm Technology Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, 
China).
Raw sequencing reads were quality-filtered using fastp (v0.24.0) to 
remove adapter sequences, low-quality reads (threshold: −q 30, −u 20), 
reads containing ambiguous bases (N > 5), and PCR duplicates, yielding 
high-quality clean reads for downstream analysis (Chen, 2023). Over­
represented rRNA fragments were removed using SortMeRNA (v4.3.6) 
(Evguenia et al., 2012). De novo assembly was conducted using 
MEGAHIT (v1.2.9) with optimized k-mer settings (k-min = 21, k-max =
141) (Li et al., 2016). Contigs shorter than 300 bp were discarded. All 
contigs ≥300 bp across samples were pooled and subjected to open 
reading frame (ORF) prediction using Prodigal (v2.6.3), and ORFs 
shorter than 300 bp were removed (Hyatt et al., 2021). Redundant se­
quences were clustered using CD-HIT (v4.8.1) at 97 % nucleotide 
identity and 90 % coverage, retaining the longest sequence in each 
cluster to generate a non-redundant gene catalog (Li and Godzik, 2006), 
with the longest sequence in each cluster retained as the representative 
to construct a non-redundant gene catalog. Functional annotation was 
performed using KofamKOALA (Kanehisa et al., 2016). To quantify gene 
expression and obtain microbial community profiles, paired-end reads 
were aligned to the non-redundant gene catalog using Salmon (v1.10.3) 
(Patro et al., 2017), and transcript abundance was reported in tran­
scripts per million (TPM).
2.5. Analytical procedures
pH, oxidation–reduction potential (ORP), and dissolved oxygen (DO) 
were measured using a digital meter (PHS–3C, INESA, China) fitted with 
corresponding probes: a pH probe (Model 501), an ORP probe (Model 
501), and a DO probe (DO-958-S), all supplied by INESA, China. Due to 
the high solids content in the effluent, liquid samples were first centri­
fuged at 6000 × g for 5  min, and the supernatant was filtered through a 
0.45  μm pore-size membrane. The resulting filtrate was used for the 
determination of soluble parameters, including SCOD and fermentation 
products. TS and VS were measured by the gravimetric method, 
involving drying at 105 ◦C and ignition at 600 ◦C. Total carbohydrate 
content was determined using the phenol–sulfuric acid method with 
glucose as the standard. Crude protein was quantified by the Kjeldahl 
method using Kjeldahl digestion vials (TNT880-CN, Hach, USA) and a 
DR3900 spectrophotometer (Hach, USA). Crude fat content was deter­
mined via the Soxhlet extraction method. Ethanol and VFAs, including 
acetic acid, propionic acid, n-butyric acid, n-valeric acid, and n-caproic 
acid, were analyzed using a gas chromatograph (GC-2014, Shimadzu, 
Japan) equipped with a capillary column (DB-FFAP, 30 m × 0.32 mm ×
1.00 µm) and a flame ionization detector (FID). LA concentrations were 
determined by high-performance liquid chromatography (LC-2030C 3D 
Plus, Shimadzu, Japan) using an InertSustain® C18 column (5  μm, 25 
cm × 4.6 mm) with ultraviolet detection at 206  nm. The mobile phase 
consisted of 85 % 20  mmol/L KH2PO4 and 15 % methanol, delivered at 
a flow rate of 0.7  mL/min. Soluble glucose was not monitored as a 
separate parameter because, under the operating conditions of this 
study, readily fermentable hexoses were expected to be rapidly 
consumed and therefore unlikely to accumulate.
2.6. Statistical analysis and figure making
Data collected during the steady-state period—defined as the stage in 
which the concentrations of main fermentation products exhibited 
relative standard deviations (RSD) of less than 20 %—were used for

subsequent analysis and comparison. Results are presented as mean ±
standard deviation and represent the fermentation performance under 
each corresponding condition. Statistical analyses were performed using 
R (version 4.3.2; RStudio version 2024.12.1) and Microsoft Excel. Dif­
ferences in means between two groups were assessed using independent 
samples t-tests, with statistical significance defined as p ≤0.05. 
Figures were generated using OriginPro 2025 and Microsoft 
PowerPoint.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Fermentation performance under different micro-aerobic conditions
3.1.1. Temporal dynamics of fermentation products under different 
aeration levels
All four fermentation reactors were operated continuously for 22 
days. Reactors A5, A15, and A40 were supplied with continuous aera­
tion throughout the entire operation, while reactor A0 was maintained 
under strictly anaerobic conditions as a control. Based on substrate 
characteristics and operating conditions, the corresponding aeration 
loads of 0, 109, 327, and 872  mL air/(gVS⋅L), respectively. And the 
reactors reached steady state on Days 10, 14, 6, and 8, respectively. At 
steady state, the DO concentrations in all reactors remained below 0.5 
mg/L. Notably, the DO levels in A0 and A5 were below the detection 
limit of the probe (<0.1  mg/L). Temporal variations in key fermentation 
products and pH throughout the experimental period are presented in 
Fig. 1a.
Immediately after fermentation was initiated, all reactors exhibited 
rapid and substantial LA accumulation, accompanied by detectable 
levels of acetic acid and ethanol. The sharp increase in organic acid 
production caused a rapid decline in pH, with values in all reactors 
dropping below 3.4 by day 8. These characteristics indicate that all 
systems rapidly entered the lactic acid-type fermentation stage 
following a short adaptation phase (Yang et al., 2021). In the early stage 
of fermentation, low concentrations of propionic acid and butyric acid 
were also detected. Notably, butyric acid concentrations gradually

(b) COD-based distribution of fermentation products. (c) Average pH and ORP values at steady state in different reactors. (d) Distribution of soluble and insoluble 
COD at steady state across reactors. (e) Hydrolysis and acidification rates under different fermentation conditions at steady state.

declined from initial values of 489–931  mg/L to nearly zero as the re­
action progressed. This phenomenon may be attributed to the poor acid 
tolerance of butyrate-producing bacteria such as Clostridium spp. 
(Esquivel-Elizondo et al., 2017), which were likely suppressed or out­
competed as pH declined.
Despite operating under strict anaerobic conditions, reactor A0 
demonstrated the fastest initial LA accumulation, reaching a peak con­
centration of 18,116  mg/L by day 6. However, the sharp pH drop (to 
3.31 on day 6) likely inhibited the activity of lactic acid bacteria (LAB), 
leading to a gradual decrease in LA concentration. The system eventu­
ally reached a steady state with a stabilized pH of 3.37 ± 0.03 and LA 
concentration maintained at 13,049 ± 1,446  mg/L. In contrast, reactors 
A5 and A15, which received low to moderate aeration, exhibited slower 
initial LA accumulation. Nevertheless, excluding short-term system 
fluctuations, both reactors showed an overall upward trend in LA con­
centration before reaching steady state. Correspondingly, their steady- 
state pH values (3.20 ± 0.03 and 3.08 ± 0.03, respectively) were 
lower than that observed in reactor A0. These observations suggest that 
low-level aeration may not accelerate the proliferation of LAB and 
facilitate rapid system start-up, but could enhance the microbial com­
munity’s tolerance to acidic conditions. This effect may be mediated by 
the induction of acid-resistance mechanisms within existing microor­
ganisms or by reshaping the community toward more acid-tolerant taxa. 
At the highest aeration rate, reactor A40 exhibited a similar trend to A0, 
with LA concentration initially increasing and then declining. However, 
unlike A0, the subsequent decrease in LA levels in A40 was likely 
attributable to the aerobic consumption of organic acids by oxygen- 
respiring microorganisms (Cao et al., 2022a). Consequently, the sys­
tem stabilized at a higher pH of 3.25 ± 0.05 compared to A5 and A15.
3.1.2. Steady-state product distribution, COD balance, and substrate 
conversion efficiency
Fig. 1b summarizes the COD-based distribution of fermentation 
products across reactors during the steady-state phase. LA was the pre­
dominant product in all systems, accounting for more than 85 % of the 
total product COD. Low-level aeration effectively enhanced LA pro­
duction. At an aeration rate of 109  mL air/(gVS⋅L), reactor A5 reached a 
steady-state LA concentration of 15,965 ± 1,405  mg/L. Further 
increasing the aeration rate to 327  mL air/(g VS⋅L) in reactor A15 
resulted in the highest LA concentration observed in this study (17,676 
± 1,135  mg/L), corresponding to an LA yield of approximately 0.40  g 
LA/g VS—representing a 35.5 % increase compared to the strictly 
anaerobic reactor A0. Under excessive aeration (A40), the LA concen­
tration dropped significantly to 10,647 ± 754  mg/L, and the acetic acid 
concentration was also lower than that observed in A15. In addition to 
LA, acetic acid and ethanol were also important fermentation products. 
Under low aeration conditions (≤327  mL air/(gVS⋅L)), the concen­
tration of acetic acid increased with rising aeration rates, whereas 
ethanol exhibited an opposite trend.
The introduction of air into the fermentation system enabled partial 
microbial oxidation of organic matter, leading to a decrease in the TCOD 
of the fermentation broth relative to the feedstock—a phenomenon 
particularly evident in reactor A40 (Fig. 1d). Despite consistent feed­
stock properties throughout the experiment, A40 exhibited a significant 
reduction in TCOD, with values approximately 26.3 % lower than those 
of A0 (p < 0.001). In contrast, TCOD changes in A5 and A15 were not 
statistically significant, likely due to their lower aeration rates.
Fig. 1e shows the HR and AR of each system during the steady-state 
phase. Before fermentation, most of the organic matter in the feedstock 
remained in the solid phase, as indicated by a low HR of 28.2 ± 0.6 %. 
Under strictly anaerobic conditions (A0), hydrolytic microorganisms 
facilitated the breakdown of solid substrates into soluble compounds, 
resulting in an average HR of 39.5 % and an AR of 34.6 %. Most of the 
solubilized organic matter was subsequently converted into fermenta­
tion products. Trace levels of aeration further enhanced substrate solu­
bilization, with reactors A5 and A15 achieving HRs of 47.0 % and 50.9 
%, respectively. The improved hydrolysis also supported more effective 
acidification, with A15 reaching the highest AR of 45.4 %. These find­
ings are consistent with previous studies showing that low-level aeration 
can stimulate the production of extracellular hydrolytic enzymes and 
enhance acidification efficiency (Cao et al., 2022b). However, when the 
aeration rate was further increased (A40), the rate of aerobic con­
sumption of organics outpaced the benefits of enhanced hydrolysis, 
leading to a marked decline in both HR and AR.
3.2. Microbial community
Based on metatranscriptomic data from steady-state samples, 
domain-level activity profiles of microbial communities under different 
aeration conditions were obtained (Fig. 2a). In previous studies, Bacteria 
have been recognized as the principal contributors to anaerobic 
fermentation, while Eukaryota are generally scarce in acidogenic sys­
tems (Zhao et al., 2024b). In line with previous findings, Bacteria 
emerged as the most transcriptionally active domain, with relative 
expression levels exceeding 90 % across all samples in current study. In 
A0, Bacteria accounted for approximately 99.1 % of the total transcripts, 
while Eukaryota represented only 0.6 %. Notably, the transcriptional 
activity of Eukaryota increased with aeration, reaching 1.0 %, 2.6 %, 
and 6.4 % in reactors A5, A15, and A40, respectively. This may be 
explained by the ability of these eukaryotic microorganisms to perform 
oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria under micro-aerobic condi­
tions, enabling more efficient energy production and thereby granting 
them a greater competitive advantage (Zimorski et al., 2019).
16S rRNA gene and ITS amplicon sequencing were performed to 
further resolve the bacterial and fungal community compositions, and 
the results are presented in Fig. 2b and Fig. 2c, respectively. Bacterial 
community profiling indicated that, across all samples, members of the 
family Lactobacillaceae—classified as LAB—predominated and served 
as the key functional guild responsible for LA production in this study. In 
A0, Lactobacillus amylolyticus was dominant (51.7 %), followed by 
Limosilactobacillus panis, Lactobacillus amylovorus, and Limosilactobacillus 
sp.; together these four LAB accounted for ~ 94.2 % of the bacterial 
community. Micro-aeration reshaped the community: in A5, relative to 
A0, L. amylovorus increased and became the dominant species (40.5 %), 
while the other three aforementioned taxa declined. Further increases in 
aeration reduced community evenness. In A15—the reactor with the 
strongest LA performance—L. amylolyticus achieved overwhelming 
dominance (86.5 %), followed by Limosilactobacillus pontis (5.7 %). 
Under the highest aeration level (A40), the bacterial community became 
further simplified, with L. amylolyticus and L. panis together comprising 
over 98 % of the total population, while all other taxa individually 
accounted for less than 0.5 %. L. amylolyticus is commonly isolated from 
strongly acidic, carbohydrate-rich fermentation environments (e.g., 
acidified malt/wort and tofu whey), and certain strains (e.g., 
L. amylolyticus L6) can maintain high viability and LA production at 
approximately pH 3 (Fei et al., 2017). Therefore, the increased abun­
dance of L. amylolyticus under micro-aeration likely enhanced the 
overall acid tolerance of the microbial community.
As shown in Fig. 2c, although ITS amplicon sequencing provided 
limited species-level resolution for fungi, it still offered a broad overview 
of the fungal community structure. In reactor A0, the community was 
relatively simple and dominated by Hyphopichia sp. (82.4 %), a member 
of the order Saccharomycetales known for performing ethanol fermen­
tation under anaerobic or hypoxic conditions (Garcia et al., 2021). In A5, 
increased aeration led to greater fungal diversity, characterized by a 
decline in Hyphopichia sp. and an expansion of other taxa, including 
uncultured Saccharomycetales and Hypomyces semicircularis. Notably, in 
A15, Holtermannia saccardoi proliferated to 17.7 % of the fungal com­
munity. This species belongs to the order Holtermanniales, members of 
which have been reported to rely primarily on aerobic respiration and to

3.3. Metatranscriptomic analysis
Through the semi-continuous micro-aeration fermentation experi­
ment, we identified the reactor A15—operated at an aeration rate of 
327  mL air/(gVS⋅L)—as achieving the highest LA yield among all tested 
conditions. This aeration level was therefore considered optimal for LA 
production from FW. To elucidate how oxygen input facilitates substrate 
hydrolysis, improves LA yield, and activates fungal metabolism, we 
performed an in-depth metatranscriptomic analysis of microbial com­
munities from the representative groups A0 (strictly anaerobic) and A15 
(optimal micro-aerated).
3.3.1. Mechanistic insights into microaeration-enhanced hydrolysis
Carbohydrates are widely recognized as the principal substrates 
metabolized by microorganisms during fermentation processes (Wang 
et al., 2020). In FW, starch and cellulose are the main carbohydrates 
(Table 1), composed of glucose units linked by glycosidic bonds (Yang 
et al., 2023). During fermentation, microbial extracellular enzymes 
hydrolyze them into oligosaccharides and monosaccharides, which then 
enter carbon metabolism pathways to form fermentation products. To 
investigate the impact of micro-aeration on carbohydrate degradation, 
the metabolic pathways for starch and cellulose hydrolysis were sum­
marized based on the KEGG database, and the transcriptional abundance 
of the corresponding hydrolytic enzymes was analyzed (Fig. 3a). In the 
diagram, solid black arrows denote community-level metabolic routes 
with strong transcriptional support, whereas dashed arrows represent 
KEGG-inferred pathways lacking detectable or appreciable transcript 
levels.
As shown in the figure, in both A0 and A15, starch degradation ap­
pears to start with the action of glucan 1,4-α-maltohydrolase (EC 
3.2.1.133), which sequentially cleaves maltose units from the non- 
reducing ends of the starch polymer. The resulting maltose is subse­
quently hydrolyzed into glucose by maltase (EC 3.2.1.20). In parallel, 
dextrins, which may be generated during partial starch breakdown, are 
further hydrolyzed by oligo-1,6-glucosidase (EC 3.2.1.10) to release 
glucose. Under optimal micro-aeration (A15), the expression levels of 
these three hydrolases were markedly elevated compared to A0, by 8.8- 
fold, 2.7-fold, and 5.9-fold, respectively. This clearly demonstrates that 
micro-aeration strongly stimulated the expression of community-level 
hydrolase genes, thereby enhancing the HR. In contrast, cellulolytic 
enzyme expression remained low across both conditions, suggesting 
minimal cellulose degradation. This observation aligns with previous 
findings that efficient cellulose utilization typically requires long HRT, 
and is rarely achieved in short-HRT acidogenic fermentation systems 
(Yang et al., 2023).
To further identify the microbial contributors responsible for starch 
hydrolysis, we analyzed the taxonomic origins of transcripts encoding 
these three key enzymes (Fig. 3b). L. amylolyticus was the predominant 
contributor to their expression. In A15, this species exhibited a marked 
increase in enzyme transcript abundance compared to A0, while other 
microbial taxa showed reduced expression. Consequently, the propor­
tion of transcripts derived from L. amylolyticus exceeded 95 % of the 
total reads assigned to these enzymes. These results suggest that micro- 
aeration not only promoted the proliferation of L. amylolyticus (as pre­
viously described in Section 3.2), but also enhanced its hydrolase 
secretion capacity. Together, these effects likely improved substrate 
availability and facilitated downstream LA production.
3.3.2. Mechanistic insights into microaeration-enhanced lactic acid 
production
Glucose released from starch hydrolysis serves as the primary sub­
strate for LA fermentation. It is metabolized by LAB mainly through 
three distinct pathways: homolactic fermentation, heterolactic fermen­
tation, and the Bifidobacteria pathway. Due to the low abundance of 
Bifidobacteria and the negligible transcriptional activity of their key 
enzymes revealed by metatranscriptomic analysis, this chapter focuses 
on analyzing and comparing the expression profiles of the homolactic 
and heterolactic fermentation pathways between A0 and A15. In addi­
tion, the mechanism by which the microbial community utilizes exog­
enous oxygen is also explored.
Both homolactic and heterolactic fermentation pathways utilize 
glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (G3P) as a key intermediate, which is 
subsequently reduced to LA via pyruvate. The main distinction lies in 
how G3P is generated: homolactic fermentation employs the glycolytic 
pathway 
(Embden–Meyerhof–Parnas,

while 
heterolactic 
fermentation relies on the phosphoketolase (PK) pathway (Wang et al.,

(except phosphogluconate dehydrogenase, EC 1.1.1.343), suggesting 
that homolactic fermentation predominated under anaerobic condi­
tions. In the micro-aerated system (A15), EMP pathway activity was 
further enhanced, as evidenced by the upregulation of related enzyme 
transcripts. Notably, transcriptional levels of pyruvate oxidase (EC 
1.2.3.3) and acetate kinase (EC 2.7.2.1) increased by 7.2-fold and 1.5- 
fold in A15, respectively, compared to A0. Pyruvate oxidase catalyzes 
the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-P using O2, generating H2O2 as a 
byproduct. Acetyl-P can then participate in substrate-level phosphory­
lation mediated by acetate kinase, producing ATP and acetic acid. 
Simultaneously, NADH peroxidase (EC 1.11.1.1)—which detoxifies 
H2O2 by converting it to H2O while consuming NADH—was upregulated 
by 3.0-fold in A15. Since NADH is typically consumed during the 
reduction of pyruvate to LA in conventional homolactic fermentation, 
this suggests that under micro-aerobic conditions, homofermentative 
LAB may reroute metabolic flux toward acetic acid production via the 
acetyl-phosphate pathway, utilizing NADH for the detoxification of 
reactive oxygen species such as H2O2.
Maintaining efficient ATP generation and appropriate NADH turn­
over is essential for fermentation performance and microbial homeo­
stasis. While ATP provides energy for cellular activities, the recycling of 
NADH is essential for maintaining metabolic flux(de Graef et al., 1999). 
Under micro-aerobic conditions, the incorporation of oxygen-responsive 
alternative pathways not only enhances ATP yield but also promotes 
NADH reoxidation, thereby maintaining intracellular redox balance. 
Specifically, the alternative shunted acetate kinase pathway converts 
acetyl phosphate to acetate with concomitant ATP production, while 
NADH peroxidase catalyzes the reduction of H2O2, thereby regenerating 
NAD+. Similar oxygen-regulated metabolic mechanisms have been re­

The actual metabolic reactions occurring in A15 are likely a composite 
of these three routes, proceeding simultaneously in specific stoichio­

Pyruvate oxidase and acetate kinase represent key enzymatic re­
sponses of homofermentative LAB to exogenous oxygen. L. amylolyticus, 
a prototypical obligate homofermentative species (Felis and Dellaglio, 
2015), was identified as the primary contributor to the transcriptional 
activity of both enzymes based on metatranscriptomic data (Fig. 4b). 
This indicates that L. amylolyticus effectively harnesses the energetic 
benefits of oxygen-driven pyruvate oxidation to acetate. The increased 
ATP yield from this pathway likely supports its robust proliferation and 
ecological dominance under micro-aerated conditions (Fig. 2b). Conse­
quently, L. amylolyticus emerged as the dominant LA producer in A15, 
accounting for 84 % of the total transcriptional abundance of L-lactate 
dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.27), compared to only 45 % in A0. This also 
explains the higher acetate production observed in A15 relative to A0.
Heterofermentative LAB are generally known to possess a complete 
enzymatic toolkit for coping with exogenous oxygen (Condon, 1987). 
Under anaerobic conditions, NADH generated via the PK pathway is 
typically used to reduce acetyl-CoA, resulting in ethanol production. 
Accordingly, the heterofermentative fermentation of 1 mol of glucose 
yields one mole of LA and 1 mol of ethanol. In the presence of oxygen, 
these organisms are capable of reoxidizing NADH via NADH oxidases, 
such as NADH:O2 oxidase (EC 1.6.3.4) or NADH:H2O2 oxidase (EC 
1.6.3.3), thereby shifting the metabolic flux toward acetate formation 
via the acetate kinase pathway and enabling additional ATP generation 
(Condon, 1987).
However, in A15, the expression levels of both NADH oxidases were 
extremely low, and most key enzymes associated with the PK pathway 
also exhibited minimal transcriptional activity. Concurrently, the 
contribution of heterofermentative LAB—including L. pontis, Limosi­
lactobacillus vaginalis, and L. panis (Felis and Dellaglio, 2015)—to the 
total transcripts encoding L-lactate dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.27) was 
lower in A15 than in A0. These findings indicate that micro-aeration did 
not promote the proliferation of heterofermentative LAB as might be 
expected based on conventional theories. One plausible explanation is 
that homofermentative LAB possess a higher affinity for oxygen,

own oxidative metabolism. This early and preferential oxygen con­

leading to their rapid proliferation and dominance in LA production. In 
contrast, heterofermentative LAB are effectively excluded from access­

lower ethanol concentrations observed in A15 compared to A0.
3.3.3. Mechanistic insights into the stimulation of eukaryotic activity by 
microaeration
Compared with strictly anaerobic conditions, prokaryotic microor­
ganisms played a more prominent role in driving community function 
under micro-aerobic conditions (Fig. 2a). Metatranscriptomic analysis 
revealed that the transcriptional abundance of genes involved in 
oxidative phosphorylation (map00190, KEGG) in sample A15 was 
approximately 30 % higher than that in A0. Furthermore, cDNA read 
origin analysis indicated that transcripts derived from eukaryotes 
increased by approximately 3.8-fold in A15 compared to A0 (Fig. 5a). 
Oxidative phosphorylation—the electron transport chain (Complexes 
I–IV) coupled to ATP synthase (Complex V)—occurs on the inner 
mitochondrial membrane. Electrons from NADH (via Complex I) and 
FADH2 (via Complex II) flow to ubiquinone, then Complex III, cyto­
chrome c, and Complex IV, which reduces O2 to H2O. Complexes I, III, 
and IV pump protons from the matrix to the intermembrane space, 
generating a proton-motive force that drives ATP synthesis by Complex 
V (Nolfi-Donegan et al., 2020). In A15, the gene expression levels of 
representative subunits of the respiratory complexes—including 
ND1–ND6 (Complex I), SdhA and SdhB (Complex II), UQCRFS1 and 
CYC1 (Complex III), COX1, COX4, COX5, and COX6 (Complex IV), as 
well as CYC (cytochrome c)—were significantly upregulated (see Sup­
plementary Material). These results collectively indicate a substantial 
enhancement in the activity of the complete eukaryotic respiratory 
chain under micro-aerobic conditions in A15. Meanwhile, the tran­
scriptional abundance of eukaryote-derived genes associated with the 
citrate cycle (TCA cycle; map00020, KEGG) in A15 was approximately 
19.6-fold higher than that in A0 (Fig. 5b). As the central hub of aerobic 
carbon metabolism, the activation of the TCA cycle supports the notion 
that eukaryotes decompose organic substrates via aerobic pathways.
To further elucidate the carbon source utilization strategies of eu­
karyotes, we analyzed the expression of gene HK, lldD, and acd, which 
encode key enzymes responsible for the initial assimilation of hexoses, 
LA, and acetic acid, respectively (Fig. 5c–e). All three enzymes were 
found to be of fungal origin, and their expression levels in A15 were 
significantly higher than those in A0. These results suggest that fungi 
exhibit enhanced uptake and assimilation of these carbon substrates 
under micro-aerobic conditions.
Taken together, the evidence indicates that under micro-aerobic 
conditions, eukaryotes—particularly fungi—assimilate glucose and 
fermentation metabolites such as LA and acetic acid, and oxidize them 
via the TCA cycle through a fully electron transport chain (ETC). When 
the aeration rate was further increased (A40), a substantial portion of

3.4. Integrative mechanistic model of micro-aeration effects on lactic acid 
fermentation
Based on the aforementioned findings, a comprehensive mechanistic 
model was developed to illustrate how micro-aeration enhances LA 
fermentation. As shown in Fig. 6, the system-level responses to exoge­
nous oxygen supply are summarized, where red arrows indicate 
fermentation steps or microbial activities that are promoted under 
micro-aerobic conditions, and green arrows represent those that are 
suppressed.
Under anaerobic conditions, LA production is jointly supported by 
homofermentative and heterofermentative LAB, with eukaryotes being 
almost entirely absent. Upon micro-aeration, oxygen enters the 
fermentation broth, triggering specific metabolic responses. For homo­
fermentative LAB, oxygen induces the activation of the pyruvate oxi­
dase–acetate kinase pathway, which diverts part of the pyruvate flux 
toward acetate formation, accompanied by the production of H2O2. This 
alternative pathway increases ATP yield, thereby supporting the pro­
liferation of homofermentative LAB. Correspondingly, NAD+ regenera­
tion shifts from the reduction of pyruvate to LA toward the reduction of 
H2O2 via NADH peroxidase. The enhanced energy yield facilitates the 
rapid 
proliferation 
of 
homofermentative 
LAB, 
particularly 
L. amylolyticus, which dominates LA production under micro-aerobic 
conditions.
Simultaneously, the presence of oxygen enables eukaryotic micro­
organisms—primarily fungi—to actively oxidize and assimilate carbon 
substrates such as glucose, LA, and acetic acid via the TCA cycle and 
ETC, resulting in high metabolic activity. However, when the aeration 
rate is excessive, overgrowth of eukaryotes leads to substantial con­
sumption of organic acid products, which in turn reduces LA yield and 
suppresses both the HR and AR of the system.
Although heterofermentative LAB possess a complete enzymatic 
toolkit to cope with exogenous oxygen and are theoretically capable of 
benefiting under aerobic conditions, they are ultimately at a disadvan­
tage. This is primarily due to their lower oxygen affinity compared to 
homofermentative LAB and fungi. Under micro-aerobic conditions, ox­
ygen is rapidly consumed by homofermentative LAB and fungi, leaving 
little or no oxygen available for heterofermentative LAB to activate their 
oxygen-dependent pathways. As a result, heterofermentative LAB 
exhibit reduced abundance and metabolic activity, ultimately losing 
their competitiveness in the micro-aerated fermentation system.
3.5. Research prospects and limitations
This study demonstrates that moderate micro-aeration can substan­
tially enhance LA fermentation from FW, leading to marked increases in 
both hydrolysis and acidification efficiencies. These findings are rele­
vant for conventional two-stage anaerobic digestion processes as well as 
for LA-oriented fermentation systems. From an engineering perspective, 
micro-aeration could in principle be implemented in existing food-waste 
anaerobic digestion plants through relatively simple retrofits (e.g., 
installation of low-rate aeration and basic control), although further 
validation and scale-up studies are still required.
At the same time, an important limitation of this work should be 
acknowledged. To ensure a constant feedstock composition throughout 
the long-term semi-continuous experiments, we used a mixture of 
commercial dog food and polished rice as a synthetic substrate. 
Although this substrate contains starch, cellulose, proteins and lipids, 
which represent the major components of real FW, its detailed compo­
sition and physical properties differ from those of real FW streams, 
whose origins and compositions are much more heterogeneous and 
time-variable. In practice, real FW may also contain higher lipid con­
tents, more recalcitrant fibrous fractions, and potential inhibitory sub­
stances (e.g., salt, seasonings and preservatives), all of which could

4. Conclusion
This study investigated the effects of different aeration rates on LA 
fermentation of FW. Micro-aeration at a rate of 327  mL air/(gVS⋅L) 
significantly enhanced LA yield, achieving approximately a 35.5 % in­
crease compared to strictly anaerobic conditions. Amplicon sequencing 
and metatranscriptomic analyses revealed that micro-aeration activated 
the pyruvate oxidase–acetate kinase pathway in homofermentative LAB, 
particularly L. amylolyticus. By converting pyruvate to acetate, these 
microorganisms gained additional ATP, which promoted their prolifer­
ation, enhanced the production of starch-degrading enzymes, and ulti­
mately improved the community’s LA production efficiency. Moreover, 
micro-aeration stimulated the proliferation of fungi and enhanced their 
ability to oxidize organic substrates. In contrast, heterofermentative LAB 
were outcompeted under micro-aerobic conditions and became 
marginalized within the fermentation system. E-supplementary data for 
this work can be found in e-version of this paper online.
